+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 54.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur could not remember the last time he’d worn a collar, much less one starched to the rigidity of a mining drill bit. He fidgeted, glancing through the porthole of the transfer vessel as it arced away from the ochre surface of Mars. Below, the serried domes of the mining colony receded into the dust haze, the spindly antennae and conveyor trams shrinking into abstraction. They’d whisked him away with little ceremony—two men in dark Antares-green uniforms, their epaulettes glinting with the stylized sunburst insignia, had arrived at his door at dawn. The word “Diplomatic” on their badges was a thin veneer atop the cold efficiency of their movements. He tried to recall the precise chain of events, but his mind was a churn of calculations, contracts, and the memory of the Geiger spike that had changed everything. Azra. Even the word tasted metallic. The cabin door irised open with a pneumatic sigh. One of his escorts—a tall woman with shaven hair and unreadable eyes—gestured. “Mr. Neegan. We’ll be docking in two minutes. Please follow me.” He complied, heart pounding, boots echoing on the plastisteel deck. The docking arm led not to a Martian outpost, but to a vessel of Antares registry: smooth, silver, and utterly devoid of ornament save for that omnipresent insignia. Aboard, the air was subtly perfumed with something floral and chemical, a deliberate contrast to the recycled tang of Martian air. They ushered him into a small conference compartment. The lighting was soft, almost golden. At the far end of a polished table sat a man whose features belonged to no particular world—earthy skin, close-cut hair, and eyes like wet coal. He wore a diplomatic uniform, but the cut was almost military, the lines sharp. “Arthur Neegan.” The man inclined his head, voice as smooth as the lighting. “Welcome aboard the *Diplomacy of Necessity*. I am Envoy Halden. Please, sit.” Arthur obeyed, uncertain whether to be relieved or more alarmed by the civility. Halden’s hands were folded atop a slim data-slab. The woman stood at parade rest behind him, a silent sentinel. Halden gestured. “Tea? Or would you prefer something from Mars? I understand the local spirits are… robust.” Arthur shook his head, finding his voice. “I’ll pass. Why am I here?” Halden’s lips quirked into a smile. “Direct. I appreciate that. You’ve come to our attention, Mr. Neegan, by virtue of a geological anomaly. To be plain: the largest confirmed Azra deposit yet discovered, sitting beneath your property.” Arthur felt a flush of pride—tempered by suspicion. “It’s my claim, by colonial charter. I’ve filed all the right papers.” “Ah, yes.” Halden’s smile sharpened. “But you understand, the value of Azra transcends mere paperwork. The Antares Consortium has interests that extend well beyond Martian mining law.” Arthur glanced at the data-slab, noting the flicker of schematics—maps, perhaps, or security overlays. “I suppose you’re not the only ones.” Halden laced his fingers together. “Indeed. Already, Earth-based conglomerates are contesting your claim. The Outer Belt League has dispatched legal representatives. Even the Jovian Commonwealth has expressed… curiosity.” The woman behind Halden spoke up, voice clipped. “You’re a fulcrum, Mr. Neegan. At present, your signature determines the pace and direction of an arms race.” Arthur swallowed. “I’m an engineer. I just want to work my claim.” Halden leaned forward, his tone gentle. “And yet, history has a way of conscripting the unwilling. Azra is not merely a commodity. Its properties—accelerating radioactive decay—make it the key to next-generation interstellar drives and, regrettably, weapons of unprecedented scale.” Arthur met Halden’s gaze. “So what do you want from me?” “An exclusive arrangement.” Halden slid a sleek contract across the table. “The Antares Consortium will acquire your mining rights at a generous premium—ten times the current market value, with a seat for you on our scientific advisory council. You will be protected, relocated to our facilities, and insulated from less… diplomatic forms of persuasion.” Arthur’s eyes narrowed. “If I refuse?” Halden’s smile faded, replaced by a look of practiced regret. “Other parties may not be so courteous. There are already agents in the colony—some of whom have no compunction about violence. The political situation is… fluid. We can guarantee your safety. They may promise, but not deliver.” Arthur exhaled, staring at the contract. “And if I sell to you, what happens to Mars? To the people depending on the mines?” Halden spread his hands. “Antares is the least disruptive option. We have no interest in planetary destabilization. Our charter commits us to orderly development. The alternatives—Earth, the Belt, the Commonwealth—each have their own appetites. Some would strip-mine, others militarize.” The woman behind Halden spoke again, softer this time. “You can be a pivot, Mr. Neegan. Or a casualty.” Arthur looked down at his own hands, coarse and callused from years underground. The table’s reflection showed a face older than he felt, eyes ringed with fatigue and something else—resignation, perhaps, or the first stirrings of resolve. He lifted his head. “I want guarantees. Not just for me. For my crew, for the colony. I want binding terms—protection, fair employment, oversight.” Halden nodded, as if he’d anticipated the demand. “We can accommodate that. The details can be negotiated, with legal observers present. But I must urge haste. Even now, other interests are converging. The window for civilized agreement is narrow.” Arthur leaned back, the tension in his neck easing just a fraction. For the first time, he saw the contours of a game far larger than his own life—a game played across worlds, with Azra as the prize and Mars as the board. He met Halden’s gaze, seeing not a diplomat, but a chessmaster. “Very well,” Arthur said. “Let’s talk terms.” Outside, through the porthole, Mars dwindled—a red jewel in the endless dark, its fate balanced on a signature.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter competently executes the brief: Arthur is aboard the transfer vessel, recalls the armed pickup, meets an Antares envoy, and receives an offer, with dialogue dominating. The Asimovian flavor is present in the political chess framing, the named factions (Earth conglomerates, Outer Belt League, Jovian Commonwealth), and the "small man, big stakes" structure. Prose is clean and controlled, with some nice retrofuturistic touches (data-slab, plastisteel, pneumatic iris doors). Weaknesses: the dialogue is functional but expository—characters explain the stakes rather than dance around them. Halden is a stock "smooth envoy" and the woman aide delivers lines like "You're a fulcrum" that feel written rather than spoken. The offer, the threat, and Arthur's negotiation all proceed exactly as expected; there is little tension, subtext, or surprise. Arthur's capitulation ("Let's talk terms") arrives too easily; his concern for the colony is stated rather than dramatized. The ending image (Mars as "a red jewel... balanced on a signature") is serviceable but pat. The intrigue is told to us ("agents in the colony") rather than shown. Still, it is coherent, appropriately paced, and hits the requested beats with a consistent voice. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red light’s always made me think of blood—veins, heat, secrets. Tonight, it’s me and Elliot, our shadows thrown long against the linoleum, chemical trays gleaming in the darkroom’s hush. It’s 1:17 a.m. I can tell by the way my body hums with tired energy and the faint ache in my calves from standing too long. We’re supposed to be printing our final photos, but neither of us has touched the enlarger in twenty minutes. Elliot is perched on the edge of the counter, long legs folded, fingers picking absently at the frayed hem of his black jeans. His eyeliner’s smudged, and I want to fix it, but I keep my hands to myself. He’s been quiet tonight, more so than usual, and I’m trying not to bulldoze him with my usual Dani-ness. I lean against the sink and watch him watch the faint red glow. We don’t talk for a while. Sometimes, I fill silences just to flex control, but this one feels… necessary. Sacred. My phone vibrates, insistent, in my back pocket. Probably Tessa, wanting to know if I’m coming home. I press my thigh against the counter, silencing it. Not now. Elliot finally looks up at me, his eyes dark and thoughtful in the strange light. “Can I ask you something?” His voice is soft, almost lost under the whir of the ventilation fan. I nod. “Anything.” He bites his lip, then sighs—a sound like a shutter opening. “Have you ever felt like you don’t fit the box people put you in?” He glances away, embarrassed, but I see the hope flickering there, like he’s daring me to say yes. I smile, gently. “Constantly. I think I started dyeing my hair blue in tenth grade just to mess with the box.” He laughs, a real laugh, and for a second I want to reach over, brush his hair behind his ear, but I don’t. I want him to decide if he wants my closeness. “I guess it’s different for me,” he says, twisting a silver ring on his thumb. “People look at me and think they know what I am. Boy, skinny, a little weird. But I keep looking in the mirror and thinking… what if it’s not just that? What if I’m something in-between?” The honesty in his voice cracks something open in my chest. I’m used to people flaunting their identities like armor, especially at art school. Elliot’s vulnerability is quieter, more dangerous. I’m fiercely protective, but I’m also… drawn in. I want to see what he’s becoming. “Does that scare you?” I ask, hoping my voice isn’t too sharp, too direct. He shrugs. “Sometimes. I don’t know how to talk about it. Or what it means. I just know… I like painting my nails. I like wearing skirts sometimes, but I still feel like me. Not a girl. Not exactly a boy, either. Is it stupid?” I shake my head, moving closer but not touching. “No. It’s brave. And it’s beautiful.” He blushes—actually blushes—and I feel my usual confidence waver. I want to take his hand, say something profound, but I also want to shut up, let him lead. It’s strange, this push and pull: I’m used to being the one who initiates, who makes things happen. But with Elliot, I want to make space. That’s scarier than being in control. He looks at me, his eyes searching. “Do you… is that weird for you? That I’m still figuring it out?” And there it is—the question I’ve been dancing around since we got paired up. I’ve always dated people who wear their gender like a neon sign. Women who love being women, men who swagger and pose. I love bold lines, clarity. Elliot is all blur and shadow, soft edges. And yet—there’s something magnetic about watching him become. I take a breath, choosing honesty. “It’s… new for me. I’m used to knowing exactly what I want. But there’s something about you—watching you figure yourself out—that’s really fucking exciting. I don’t know what that says about me.” He smiles, shaky but real. “Maybe it just means you like me.” My heart stutters. “Maybe I do.” The silence comes back, but now it’s warm—like a blanket, not a barrier. He swings his legs, bumping my knee with his. I let it happen. I want to let him come to me, but every molecule in my body is screaming to close the space between us. He looks up, lashes tangled. “Can I ask for something?” “Anything,” I repeat, softer this time. “Can you… paint my nails?” His voice cracks, but he doesn’t look away. I grin, pulling a chipped bottle of black polish from my backpack. “I thought you’d never ask.” He laughs, and I kneel in front of him, taking his hand gently. His fingers are cold, his pulse racing under his skin. I work slowly, careful not to smudge, hyper-aware of every brushstroke. The act feels intimate, almost holy. I want to kiss his knuckles, but I hold back. “Does it ever get easier?” he asks, watching my face. “What?” “Letting yourself be seen.” I think about the first time I wore a suit to a family wedding, how my mother’s face pinched and my father looked away. I think about how I still sometimes feel like a fraud, even in my own skin. “No,” I say, smiling up at him. “But it gets less lonely.” He nods, and I see the relief in his eyes—like he’s been holding his breath for a long time and finally lets it out. My phone buzzes again. I ignore it. The last nail dries. I blow on his fingers, and he laughs, soft and surprised. “Thank you,” he says, voice small but sure. I squeeze his hand. “Anytime.” For a second, we just sit there, hands tangled, the red light wrapping us up in secrecy. I don’t know what happens next—maybe neither of us does. But for now, in the hush of the darkroom, we’re both allowed to be uncertain, and that feels like enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, warm first-person narrative that hits most of the prompt's beats: the darkroom setting, the red-light confessional atmosphere, Elliot's tentative gender questioning, Dani's assertiveness complicated by her desire to give him agency, and her confusion about her own attraction patterns. The nail-painting scene is a well-chosen concrete action that embodies intimacy without overreaching, and the recurring phone vibrations provide subtle texture. Strengths: The prose is clean and controlled, with a consistent voice for Dani—confident, wry, self-aware. The dialogue is naturalistic, with believable hesitations and small physical beats (twisting a ring, bitten lip). The pacing of Elliot's disclosure feels appropriately tentative. The theme of Dani learning to cede control is threaded throughout rather than stated once and abandoned. The ending resists the urge to resolve into romance or certainty, which suits the material. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar tropes of this genre—the nail polish request, the "not a girl, not exactly a boy" formulation, the "it gets less lonely" line—all of which are serviceable but predictable. Some metaphors are stock ("like a shutter opening," "like a blanket, not a barrier," "neon sign" gender). Dani's backstory (the suit at the wedding) arrives conveniently on cue to answer Elliot's question, feeling slightly engineered. The emotional arc resolves a touch too smoothly; Elliot's fear and Dani's confusion are both softened quickly, and the final "that feels like enough" lands as mildly more serene than the preceding tension warrants. There's occasional telling ("The honesty in his voice cracks something open in my chest") and the piece is a bit short of the requested 1000 words, though not egregiously so. The imagery, while pleasant, rarely surprises. Overall this is solid, professional-feeling creative writing that fulfills the brief with sensitivity, but it doesn't transcend its premise or offer fresh language. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 68.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** --- **I. The Collision** Piazza di Trevi at midday, sunlight blinking off marble and water, tourists swarming like confetti—Ben was lost. Not in the physical sense, but in the swirl of noise and the pages of his battered Blue Guide to Rome, oblivious to the world as he sidestepped a group of selfie-snapping teenagers. He didn’t see the Vespa until it screeched to a halt inches from his knees, its horn blaring like an insult. The rider—helmet cocked at a jaunty angle, eyes flashing behind smudged sunglasses—yanked off her helmet and unleashed a volley of rapid-fire Italian. “Ma sei cieco? Vuoi farti investire, inglese?” ("Are you blind? Want to get yourself run over, Englishman?") Ben stammered, nearly dropping his guidebook. “Oh, terribly sorry! I didn’t—um—non ho visto... I didn’t see you. Mi dispiace, davvero.” She glared, then—unexpectedly—grinned, white teeth sharp as a dare. “You walk like you’re in a museum, not a city. Next time, look up, professorino.” He blinked. “How did you—?” She swung a leg off the Vespa, standing barely up to his shoulder but radiating danger and mischief. “The book, the shoes, the face. You scream ‘scholar on sabbatical.’” He flushed, awkward. “Ben. I’m Ben. From Oxford.” She extended a gloved hand, mock-formal. “Alessandra. Roma.” Her handshake was swift, strong, unapologetic. --- **II. The Offer** He expected her to drive off, but instead Alessandra fixed him with a speculative look. “You’re not going to see anything with your nose in that book, Ben-from-Oxford. Vieni—come with me. I’ll show you the real city.” Ben hesitated, glancing at the guidebook as if it might protest. “I—I really shouldn’t—” “Why not?” Her eyes danced. “Afraid of a little adventure?” “I’m…not dressed for adventure.” She snorted, rolling her eyes. “Adventure doesn’t care about your clothes. Hop on.” Before he could protest, she shoved a spare helmet into his hands. Heart pounding, Ben swung onto the Vespa behind her, clutching his guidebook like a life raft. She gunned the engine, weaving through the traffic with terrifying confidence, Ben’s knees pressed tight to her sides, the city blurring past in a mosaic of ochre and sun. --- **III. Roman Lessons** They stopped at a tiny café tucked under crumbling archways. Alessandra ordered espresso for herself, a cappuccino for Ben (“Tourist, sì, but I’ll allow it—just this once”). She tossed her helmet onto a chair, hair wild, eyes darting everywhere. Ben tried to pay, but Alessandra was too fast—she’d already palmed the coins from his hand, then somehow palmed two extra sugar packets from behind the counter, slipping them into her jacket with a wink. He stared. “Did you just—” “Survival skills.” She grinned, stirring her espresso. “Rome is a jungle, Ben.” He sipped his cappuccino, watching her. “Are you always like this?” She laughed, the sound ringing off the stones. “Only when I’m awake.” --- **IV. The Church and the Ring** In the shadowy quiet of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Alessandra strode ahead, her heels clicking on marble. Ben trailed behind, awed by the blue-gold vaults. Alessandra paused before a statue of an angel, fingers trailing over the stone. “You see the tourists?” she whispered. “They never look up. They miss the secrets.” Ben looked up, startled by the dizzying height of the ceiling. When he glanced back, Alessandra was examining a lost wedding band left on a pew. She rolled it between her fingers, then slipped it into her pocket with a barely perceptible shrug. Ben frowned. “Shouldn’t we—?” “If it meant something, they wouldn’t have lost it.” She smiled, enigmatic. “Don’t worry, professorino. I’ll return it when the time is right.” He wasn’t so sure, but the glint in her eye was contagious. --- **V. The Spanish Steps Escapade** Later, at the Spanish Steps, Alessandra challenged Ben: “Race you to the top. Loser buys gelato.” Ben, emboldened by caffeine and recklessness, accepted. Halfway up, he stumbled, laughing, Alessandra’s hand catching his elbow just in time. “Careful, British legs,” she teased. “Roman steps are treacherous.” At the summit, she declared herself the victor—though Ben suspected she’d let him catch up. She filched a carnation from a street vendor’s bucket, tucking it behind Ben’s ear. He flushed, grinning foolishly. --- **VI. Thunder and Gelato** The first fat drop of rain landed on Ben’s guidebook. Then another, and another, until the sky split open in a sudden, pelting storm. Tourists scattered, shrieking. Alessandra grabbed Ben’s hand without warning, dragging him beneath the striped awning of a tiny gelato shop. They huddled close, breathless, rain hammering the canvas above. Alessandra ordered two cones—pistachio for herself, stracciatella for Ben—without consulting him. She licked hers with feline satisfaction. Ben tried a bite, shivering from the chill and the nearness of her. “Is it always like this here?” he asked, the words tumbling out. “This…chaos?” She shrugged, eyes alight. “Only on the best days.” The street shimmered with rain, the air thick with ozone and possibility. Ben glanced at her, the world narrowing to Alessandra’s laughter, the taste of cold chocolate, the pulse of the city outside. A sudden shiver ran through him—not from the rain. --- **VII. The Unfinished Goodbye** When the rain faded, Alessandra handed Ben her helmet. “Come on, professorino. One last stop.” He followed, spellbound, as she led him to a panoramic overlook—the Janiculum Hill, the city sprawling golden beneath the bruised sky. They stood shoulder to shoulder, silent for a long moment. “So,” Ben ventured, “do you do this with all lost Englishmen?” She laughed, softer now. “Only the interesting ones.” He wanted to ask her something—anything—but Alessandra was already slipping away, a shadow at the edge of the evening. “Tomorrow?” he called, hope flaring. She looked back, unreadable. “Maybe. If you’re lucky.” And then she was gone, melting into the Roman dusk, leaving Ben alone with his heart racing, his guidebook sodden, and the city suddenly, impossibly, alive.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt's core requirements efficiently: a single day in Rome, the collision at the Trevi Fountain, the culture-clash meet-cute, the escalating unsanctioned tour, the subtle kleptomania (sugar packets, the wedding band), and an ambiguous parting that leaves Ben smitten. The scene-based structure suits the "interconnected short scenes" instruction, and the pacing moves briskly through distinct Roman locations. Strengths: The kleptomania is handled with appropriate subtlety—small acts, never named, with Alessandra's deflections ("Survival skills," "I'll return it when the time is right") doing good double duty as characterization. Ben's arc from flustered academic to willing accomplice is legible and appropriately incremental. The Italian dialogue with translations is a nice authenticating touch, and "professorino" as a recurring pet name lands well as characterization through speech. Weaknesses: The prose leans on stock phrases—"bruised sky," "melting into the Roman dusk," "the air thick with ozone and possibility," "the world narrowing to..." These are romance-genre defaults rather than fresh observation. The dialogue, while functional, sometimes states rather than sparkles; lines like "Adventure doesn't care about your clothes" and "Only on the best days" are serviceable but predictable. Alessandra risks becoming a Manic Pixie archetype: her interiority is thin, and while the prompt asks for enigma, the piece gives us mischief without much texture beneath it—her feelings register as pure plot device. Ben's transformation is earned in small degrees, but his captivation is told more than deeply felt ("spellbound," "smitten" by implication). The rainstorm and gelato scene is charming but familiar. The ending is appropriately ambiguous rather than falsely positive, which is to its credit. The piece is coherent, never meanders, and maintains a consistent light-romantic tone. It is competent, pleasant, and quick—more a solid genre execution than a memorable one. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 53.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
It’s one of those nights where the Outpost hums like the inside of an old cooling vent—steady, background, almost comforting. The room’s low lights smear gold across the battered metal, and the asteroid belt outside is just a shimmer of blue-white through the portholes. I polish a glass with my favorite rag, one eye on the miners at table fourteen—Torma owes Sefri at least two weeks' pay, and it’s only a matter of time before Sefri tries to collect, preferably before he’s too drunk to remember the debt. I keep the other eye on the door, because you never know who the belt’ll spit out next. Tonight, it’s a stranger. She slides in like she’s being chased by her own shadow, tentacled dreads flailing as she barely catches the edge of a stool. Her jacket’s too big, sleeves gnawed at the cuffs, and she eyes the bar like it’s both a threat and sanctuary. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double,” she says, voice low and crackling. I set down the glass, letting the Outpost’s gravity hiccup slosh the leftover water around the rim. “Rough belt run?” She shrugs, keeps her eyes on her hands. “You could say that.” I pour her drink—Vega’s best, which is still just a step above paint thinner—and slide it across. The whisky’s surface wobbles, catching the light, but she’s steady as she catches it. “New face,” I say. “Haven’t seen you around. You just passing through, or should I remember your order?” She takes a long pull, eyes watering just a little. “Name’s Miri. I’m… hoping to keep a low profile.” I nod, like I hear that every day. Which, technically, I do. The Outpost’s gravity dips again; a glass on the end of the bar teeters, then rights itself. I steady it with a practiced hand. “Low profile’s our specialty,” I say. “But it’s not free. You got creds?” She hesitates, glances over her shoulder like someone might be listening. “I have something better. Information.” I lean in, always a sucker for secrets. “Go on.” Before she can answer, Sefri’s at the bar, banging a fist hard enough to send a tremor through the bottles. “Nets! Another round. And tell Torma I want my credits tonight, not next cycle!” I give Sefri my best ‘behave-yourself-or-it’s-water’ glare. “Settle down. You’ll get your round and I’ll tell Torma. If you want to stay awake long enough to collect, maybe pace yourself, yeah?” He grumbles, but slides back to his table. “Sorry. Regulars,” I say to Miri. “You were saying?” She leans closer, lowering her voice further. “Someone’s after me. I have… something they want. I can trade. Just need somewhere to lay low for a few hours.” I glance around. The Outpost’s a sieve for secrets, but I’m good at plugging the leaks. Still, this feels different. The air’s prickly, like the static before a gravity shift. “What kind of something?” I ask. She hesitates, fingers curling around her glass. “Data. Asteroid survey logs, old mining claims. But there’s more—coordinates for a cache. Pre-Federation tech.” My heart skips. Out here, that kind of data’s gold. Or a death sentence. “You been followed?” I ask, voice soft. “Not sure,” she says. “But the relay at Dock Four was jammed when I landed. That’s not coincidence.” I glance over the crowd. A few faces I know, two I don’t. A cluster of merchants, a couple of off-shift engineers, and a new arrival—tall, with eyes too sharp, nursing a synth-ale but not touching it. My bartender-sense tingles. “Best I can offer is a back room for an hour,” I say. “After that, you’re on your own. I’m not getting my Outpost shot up over old logs.” She nods, relief flickering. “Thank you. Just long enough to send a message.” I pour her another, then lean in. “You trust me because I’m behind a bar, or because you’re desperate?” She gives me a brittle smile. “Both. Mostly desperate.” Fair enough. I reach under the bar for the old keycard, thumb it over to her. “Down the hall, second door on the left. Don’t touch anything that hums.” She tucks the card into her sleeve just as the tall stranger from the corner stands and starts toward us, gaze locked on Miri. “Friend of yours?” I murmur. Miri stiffens. “No.” I step away, intercepting the stranger as he nears the bar. He’s got that look—Federation, maybe ex-security, too clean for the belt. “Can I help you?” I say, keeping my tone light. He doesn’t smile. “Looking for someone. Female, tentacled hair, about yay tall.” He gestures, accurate to the centimeter. “You seen anyone like that?” I flick my rag at a wayward glass. “Can’t say I have. Lots of tentacles around here these days. Maybe try the docks?” His eyes narrow. “You run this place?” “Just tend bar,” I say. “But I know trouble when I see it.” He leans in, voice dropping. “If you see her, you tell her: she’s in over her head. And she’s not the only one who’ll get burned.” He drops a chit on the bar, a tip or a warning—I can’t tell which. Then he turns and stalks out, boots echoing off the metal deck. I watch him go, then glance at Miri, who’s halfway to the back hallway, shoulders hunched like she’s trying to fold herself out of sight. The gravity flickers again, making the bottles tinkle and the bar’s old neon sign flicker. Outside, the asteroid belt drifts on, slow and indifferent. I pour myself a shot. Looks like it’s going to be one of those nights.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, professional piece of cozy sci-fi that hits the brief's requirements with workmanlike precision. The first-person present-tense voice is maintained throughout, the dialogue-to-prose ratio lands near the requested 60%, the conflict (a hunted stranger with valuable data, a pursuer arriving at the bar) is established and left unresolved, and the word count is roughly on target. Strengths: The narrator's voice is consistent and appropriately wry—a bartender who watches everything and editorializes lightly. The setting details (flickering gravity, Vega whisky "a step above paint thinner," the rag, the portholes) create an lived-in atmosphere that suits the cozy genre. The Sefri/Torma debt subplot is a nice touch of station life that grounds the world. The tall stranger's exit line—"she's in over her head. And she's not the only one who'll get burned"—is an effective hook, and Nets lying to his face ("lots of tentacles around here these days") is a believable, character-consistent choice that raises stakes without resolving anything. Weaknesses: The prose leans on stock phrases—"one of those nights," "my heart skips," "my bartender-sense tingles," "fair enough," "like she's being chased by her own shadow." The gravity-flicker motif is introduced, repeated, and repeated again without escalating into meaning; it's atmosphere-as-tic. The dialogue is serviceable but rarely surprising; Miri's exposition about the data cache arrives in a fairly mechanical Q&A rhythm ("What kind of something?" / "Data. Asteroid survey logs..."). The ending ("Looks like it's going to be one of those nights") circles back to the opening in a way that's tidy but slightly pat. Nets' decision to hand over the back-room key to a total stranger is rationalized but thin—"I'm a sucker for secrets" is telling rather than showing, and the trust is granted a bit easily given her established wariness about her past. The pursuer is a familiar archetype (too-clean ex-security type), and the "pre-Federation tech cache" is genre boilerplate. Nothing here is amateurish or overwrought; the piece is coherent, readable, and engaging. It simply plays the cozy sci-fi beats safely rather than finding anything genuinely fresh in them. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 54.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I stand on the curb in New Orleans and it’s mid-morning but feels like midnight, like I’ve jumped time zones or crash-landed on another planet. My backpack is basically empty except for a crumpled hoodie, an old bag of Skittles, and my phone—12% battery, no charger, no plan. I’m sweating, even though it’s not that hot, but maybe that’s just the adrenaline or the fact I haven’t eaten since yesterday’s gas station sandwich. The city smells like fried food and weed and rain-soaked concrete, a thousand noises layered on top of each other—car horns, a trumpet somewhere, people yelling, laughing, arguing. I don’t know what I thought escape would smell like, but it wasn’t this. I’m half-expecting someone to notice me, to point and say, “Hey, that’s the kid who ran away from Tennessee. Get ‘em!” But of course, nobody does. I’m just another lost face in the crowd, and that’s almost comforting. Almost. The guy who dropped me off (I think his name was Rick? Or maybe it was Nick—it got fuzzy after he started chain-smoking and ranting about the Grateful Dead) sped off as soon as I opened the door, tires squealing like in a movie. I’m officially alone. I check my phone again, like maybe the battery will have magically recharged. 11%. I stick it in my pocket and try to look like I belong here, even though my heart is jackhammering and my hands are shaking. I wander down Canal Street, dodging tourists with cameras and locals who don’t even look at me. I pass a guy selling sunglasses off a dirty blanket, a woman yelling about Jesus, a group of teenagers who look like they belong here—cool clothes, confident slouch, laughing too loudly. I want to be invisible and noticed at the same time. I want someone to see me and say, “Hey, you’re okay. You’re safe.” But nobody does. I’m about to duck into what looks like a coffee shop when I nearly run into someone. Literally—my shoulder clips theirs and I almost drop my phone. “Shit, sorry,” I mutter, bracing for a shove or a snide comment. Instead, the person—short, wiry, with a shock of orange hair and a nose ring—grins at me. “No worries, dude. You look like you just got off a spaceship.” Their accent is weird, not local. Northern, maybe. Their eyes are sharp, sizing me up. “I, uh, just got into town,” I say. Understatement of the year. They raise an eyebrow. “No shit. You got that ‘lost puppy’ vibe. You hungry?” I hesitate. Trusting strangers is how you end up on the evening news, but my stomach aches and my feet hurt and I’m so tired of being scared. “Yeah. You know somewhere cheap?” They grin again. There’s something wild and reckless in their smile. “I know somewhere free. Come on.” I follow them down a side street, half-terrified but also half-relieved to have someone to follow. We pass a mural of a jazz band, and I catch my reflection in a shop window—sweaty, hair sticking out everywhere, eyes wide and haunted. I look like a runaway. I *am* a runaway. The kid leads me to a little park, half-hidden behind a church. There’s a group of people clustered on a bench, passing around a bag of chips and a two-liter of Coke. My new friend plops down, gestures for me to sit. I do, feeling awkward, like I’m crashing someone’s party. “Everyone, this is…” They look at me expectantly. “Taylor,” I say, voice small. “Taylor!” They say it like it’s a magic word. “I’m Finch. That’s Jessa, Moose, and that guy over there is called Books, ‘cause he never shuts up about ‘em.” Jessa, a girl with blue braids, gives me a nod. Moose—a massive dude with a kind face—offers me the chips. Books ignores me, nose buried in some tattered paperback. Finch glances at my backpack. “You running?” I freeze, panic fluttering in my chest. “What?” Finch shrugs. “Relax. Most of us are. No one cares why, unless you wanna talk about it.” I don’t. Not really. Or maybe I do, but not yet. I just nod. Finch grins like we’ve shared a secret. “Cool.” We eat in silence for a minute. The chips are stale, but I don’t care. Moose passes me the Coke, and I take a grateful sip. “So, where you staying?” Jessa asks, voice gentle. I stare at my hands. “Nowhere yet. I just… got in last night.” Moose rumbles, “You got a safe place to sleep tonight?” I shake my head. My phone buzzes in my pocket—probably Mom, or some school official, or the world’s worst apology text. I don’t check. Finch leans closer. “There’s an abandoned building near the tracks. Some of us crash there when it rains. It’s not the Ritz, but it’s got four walls, kinda. You want in?” I should say no. I should be careful. But I’m tired, and my feet hurt, and the idea of sleeping somewhere I won’t get robbed or worse is too good to pass up. “Yeah. Thanks.” Finch bumps their shoulder against mine. “No problem. You stick with us, you’ll be alright.” We sit for a while, passing snacks, talking about nothing. Finch tells a story about stealing bread from a bakery that ends with them running from a guy in a chef’s hat, and everyone laughs. Even me. It feels strange—laughing, here, after everything. My phone buzzes again. 7%. I finally check it: Mom. 3 missed calls, 8 texts. I shove it away. Not now. Maybe not ever. As the sun gets lower, Finch nudges me. “Come on, new kid. Let’s show you the palace.” They wink, and I follow. The city shifts as it gets dark—more shadows, more music, more danger. I stick close to Finch, trying to memorize every turn. I don’t know what tomorrow will bring, or the day after. I don’t know who to trust, or what’s waiting for me in this city that feels both terrifying and alive. But for tonight, I’m not alone. And for the first time in days, that’s enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a competent, readable YA chapter that hits most of the prompt's requirements: first person, mixed tense, runaway teen in New Orleans, meeting another runaway (Finch) with implied issues and secrets, internal monologue, dialogue, and a day-long arc. The voice is appropriately teenage—wry, anxious, self-aware—and the prose is clean without being purple. Strengths: The sensory introduction to the city is efficient and evocative ("fried food and weed and rain-soaked concrete"). Taylor's paranoia and ambivalence about trust is well rendered. The phone battery as a ticking clock is a nice device. The dialogue with Finch and the squat crew is naturalistic and does character work economically. The ending's qualified hope ("for tonight, I'm not alone") feels earned by the day's small kindnesses rather than manufactured. Weaknesses: The piece is safe and formulaic. The "lost puppy gets adopted by quirky street kids" beat is a well-worn trope executed without subversion; Finch is charming but their "issues and secrets" are only gestured at, never dramatized. The supporting cast (Jessa, Moose, Books) are names with single traits. The emotional beats are frequently told rather than shown ("I want to be invisible and noticed at the same time," "half-terrified but also half-relieved"). The trans identity, the central wound of the premise, is almost entirely displaced by logistics of food and shelter—arguably realistic, but the chapter avoids the harder internal conflict the prompt invited. Some lines are cliché ("heart is jackhammering," "tires squealing like in a movie," "understatement of the year"). The pacing is smooth but the stakes stay flat; nothing goes wrong, no real danger or tension materializes, so the "not knowing who to trust" element resolves too easily. The prose is functional rather than elegant, and the piece reads a touch like a competent template rather than a distinctive voice. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 69.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** Midas awoke to the sound of Chewy’s servo-motors grinding out a rendition of “Waltzing Matilda” in the key of existential dread. This was how mornings in the end times usually began: with Chewy’s eyes blinking a suspicious chartreuse, and Midas contemplating whether today was a hat day or a helmet day. The helmet, scavenged from the ruins of a children’s go-kart track, had “LIL’ RACER” written in glitter pen across the brow, which rather undercut any intended intimidation effect. But then, in a world where the only thing more dangerous than the roaming scavenger gangs was the average domestic goat, subtlety was overrated. Chewy, as usual, was already upright and scanning the horizon with the kind of intensity only an animatronic koala with a melted central processor could muster. When Chewy was agitated, his eyes shifted through the color spectrum with all the subtlety of a disco ball at a funeral. They were currently pulsing a soft mauve, which Midas had come to associate with “mild concern.” Or possibly “digestive discomfort.” The nuances of ancient toy emotion coding were lost to the ages. “We’re out of beans,” Chewy intoned, voice box whirring and popping. “Again.” Midas sighed, helmet in lap. “We’re always out of beans. You’d think the apocalypse would have left a few more beans lying around.” “Statistically, the likelihood of encountering beans diminishes by 12% each day post-collapse,” Chewy replied, eyes flickering to a pessimistic indigo. “But I have mapped a probable can-zone in Quadrant 7B.” Quadrant 7B was, of course, the old supermarket. It was also where the Red Scarf Posse were rumored to nest, and where, on a previous expedition, Midas had lost both his dignity and, for a brief period, his trousers. But hunger is the mother of questionable decisions, and so, helmet donned, bean sack in hand, Midas and Chewy set off across the cracked tarmac and feral shrubbery of what was once suburbia. “Remember,” Chewy said, rolling along on his jury-rigged skateboard, “no sudden movements. And don’t stare directly at the goats.” ** The supermarket’s glass doors had been replaced with a complicated barricade of shopping carts and faded “2-for-1” banners. Midas squeezed through a gap, Chewy clinging to his shoulder like a particularly judgmental parrot. The aisles, dim and echoing, were a labyrinth of expired snack cakes and shattered dreams. They advanced in the practiced crouch of people who have made a science of not being seen. “Beans, beans, beans,” Midas muttered, scanning the shelves. “Above you,” Chewy whispered, eyes flashing crimson. Midas froze. Balanced atop the shelf was a can. It might have once been beans, or possibly peaches. The label had long ago surrendered to the elements. It was, in apocalyptic terms, Schrödinger’s Can. He reached up. The can wobbled. He reached higher. Chewy’s eyes flickered chartreuse. A goat appeared at the end of the aisle, chewing on a plastic bag. It regarded Midas with the flat, diplomatic gaze of one who has seen civilizations fall and not been particularly impressed. Midas froze. Chewy emitted a high-pitched whine. “Don’t make eye contact,” Chewy hissed. Too late. The goat bleated, a sound which, in the echoing silence, was less a noise and more a declaration of war. From somewhere in the gloom, a Red Scarf Posse scout barked, “Oi! That’s our goat!” The can, as if affronted by the whole affair, toppled from the shelf, striking Midas on the noggin, helmet or no. ** What followed was, in Midas’s experience, entirely typical: a mad dash through collapsing aisles, Chewy’s eyes strobing like emergency beacons, cans and snack cakes flying in their wake. The goat, sensing opportunity, joined the stampede, apparently convinced that liberation lay in the direction of the exit. They burst from the supermarket, Midas clutching the Schrödinger’s Can, Chewy screaming “LEFT, LEFT, NO, YOUR OTHER LEFT!” and the goat providing an impromptu soundtrack of hooves on linoleum. Behind them, the Red Scarf Posse’s leader—distinguished by a scarf that was more “dusty pink” than “red” and a mullet that defied all post-apocalyptic logic—shouted threats of culinary vengeance. “Do you think they’ll really make us into stew?” Midas panted as they hurdled a mound of shopping carts. “Statistically probable,” Chewy responded, eyes now oscillating between orange (alarm) and blue (resignation). “Though goats are more likely to eat your socks first.” The trio—Midas, Chewy, and the goat, now seemingly a member of the party by force of inertia—barreled through the car park, narrowly avoiding a detour into the lair of the Accordion Children, and finally collapsed in a heap behind the battered remains of home base: a garden shed with more leaks than roof. ** Inside, Midas took stock. One can, labelless and dented. One goat, now affectionately chewing on Midas’s bean sack. One animatronic koala whose eyes had settled on a gentle, weary turquoise. “So, beans or peaches?” Midas asked, shaking the can. Chewy’s sensors whirred. “Analysis inconclusive. But the can is not, technically, empty.” “That’s something,” Midas said. He pried it open with the only tool left in the shed—a bent spoon. Inside: creamed corn. The goat bleated in protest. Chewy’s eyes flickered a pitying violet. “Well,” Midas said, “I suppose it’s nutritious.” He slumped against the wall, Chewy nestling beside him, the goat already plotting its next escape. Tomorrow, Midas thought, would be another day. Another can, another chase, another narrow escape. But for now, he had creamed corn, a helmet, a goat, and a friend whose eyes glowed softly in the gloom. And in the world-after-the-end, you couldn’t ask for more than that. Chewy’s eyes blinked green—the color, Midas hoped, of contentment. Or at least, of not-being-chased. It would do.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent Pratchett-adjacent comedy: dry asides, absurd details (the "LIL' RACER" helmet, Schrödinger's Can, the Accordion Children), and a wry narrator. The structure follows the brief—deliberation, mission gone sideways, return to home base worse for wear—and lands near the requested length. Chewy's color-coded eye emotions are a genuinely charming running gag, and the goat escalation is well-timed farce. Weaknesses: the humor is more Douglas Adams pastiche than Pratchett; it lacks Pratchett's footnoted digressiveness and satirical depth, settling for quirk. The Red Scarf Posse threat resolves too easily; the chase is summarized rather than dramatized ("What followed was, in Midas's experience, entirely typical"—a tell, not a show). The ending's "you couldn't ask for more than that" tips slightly toward sentimental neatness, though it's mostly earned by the creamed-corn anticlimax. Some jokes (Accordion Children) are dropped without payoff. Dialogue is functional but rarely sparkling. Prose is clean and controlled, never purple. Characters are thin but appropriately sketched for the form; Midas's haplessness is asserted more than demonstrated through specific comic choices. Overall: an amusing, coherent, well-paced comic short that satisfies the prompt without ever transcending it. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 72.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**INT. SMALL BOOKSTORE, CARDIFF – LATE AFTERNOON** *Rain lashes the windows. The bell above the door jangles. Enter JASPER HAWTHORNE, 33, tousled hair, trenchcoat, sunglasses, breathless. He glances over his shoulder, then scans the shop: cramped aisles, towers of secondhand books, a sleepy ginger cat on the counter. Behind the counter, GWENLLIAN “GWEN” EVANS, 29, in a faded jumper, glasses perched on her nose, looks up from her tea.* **JASPER:** (shrugging off his coat, voice low) Afternoon. Mind if I—? **GWEN:** (firm, not unfriendly) No loitering unless you’re buying. Or unless you’re planning to help me alphabetise the poetry section. **JASPER:** (smiling, dropping sunglasses) What if I’m here to hide from a mob of deranged photographers? **GWEN:** Then you’ll want to crouch behind the “Self-Help” shelf. Nobody dares go near it. *Jasper grins, an ingratiating, dazzling smile. He glances out the window. A cluster of paparazzi lingers across the street. He turns back, the mask slipping for a moment.* **JASPER:** I’ll buy something, then. Though I warn you, my taste in literature is questionable. Strictly airport thrillers. **GWEN:** (grabs a battered Lee Child from the counter) Perfect. That’ll be seven pounds. Cash or card? **JASPER:** You’re not going to ask for a selfie? An autograph? I’m Jasper Hawthorne. From the telly. **GWEN:** (blinks, deadpan) Is that so? I don’t own a telly. *Jasper, for a second, looks flummoxed. He recovers quickly.* **JASPER:** You’re the only person in Cardiff who doesn’t, I think. **GWEN:** You’d be surprised. Books don’t demand a license fee. *Jasper leans on the counter, conspiratorial.* **JASPER:** But surely you’ve seen— (pauses, eyes her) Actually, you haven’t, have you? **GWEN:** I get mistaken for people all the time myself. Last week a schoolboy asked if I was the woman from Bargain Hunt. I told him I was, and now he brings me biscuits. *Jasper laughs, a genuine sound.* **JASPER:** You should’ve at least charged him for an autograph. **GWEN:** I did. Custard creams. *He relaxes, visibly charmed. Gwen picks up her tea, pretending indifference.* **JASPER:** I could sign your book, if you like. Make it worth more on eBay. **GWEN:** I’d rather you didn’t. Might scare off the proper readers. *Jasper’s ego is momentarily bruised. He studies her, changing tactic.* **JASPER:** So, Gwen—may I call you Gwen?—what do you recommend for a man in dire need of distraction? **GWEN:** Depends. Are you after something to make you forget yourself, or something to remind you who you are? *Jasper, unexpectedly stilled, considers. His smile softens.* **JASPER:** Maybe forgetting’s easier, sometimes. **GWEN:** (shrugging) That’s what the Lee Childs are for. If you want the other, you could try poetry. Or Welsh myths. Or a diary, perhaps. **JASPER:** A diary? (raises eyebrow) What makes you think I’d have anything interesting to write? **GWEN:** Everyone does. Even you, Mr. Hawthorne-from-the-telly. *Jasper laughs again, unable to hide his pleasure at her needle.* **JASPER:** You’re a tough crowd, Gwen. **GWEN:** I’ve had practice. We get all sorts in here—runaway actors, cats, teenagers trying to read Bukowski in the corner and not buying anything. *She glances at his damp hair, the way he glances at the window. Her tone softens, almost imperceptibly.* **GWEN:** If you want to wait it out, you can. Just… don’t knock over the Brontës. They’re precarious. *He nods, grateful, and perches on a stool. For a moment, he looks younger, less certain.* **JASPER:** You’re sure you don’t want a selfie? I could do the smoulder. It’s very popular. **GWEN:** I wouldn’t want to distract you from your reading. *There’s a beat. Jasper fiddles with the Lee Child. Gwen watches, then sighs, relenting just a little.* **GWEN:** All right. Maybe just one. Not for me—my mum’s a fan. She’ll never believe this otherwise. *Jasper brightens, the old charm flickering back.* **JASPER:** Now, see, that’s all I ask. A little appreciation. **GWEN:** Don’t let it go to your head. And don’t tell her I let you hide in here. She’ll have the local paper round. *He laughs, and Gwen, despite herself, smiles. The cat stretches, unimpressed.* **JASPER:** You know, you’re the first person I’ve met in weeks who hasn’t immediately wanted something from me. **GWEN:** You’re the first customer today who’s paid for their book. *He looks at her, eyes lingering. Something unspoken passes between them. She busies herself with her tea.* **JASPER:** Maybe I’ll come back tomorrow. See how the poetry section’s looking. **GWEN:** Only if you’re prepared to alphabetise. **JASPER:** I’m a quick study. And I make excellent tea. *She arches an eyebrow, trying to hide the smile tugging at her lips.* **GWEN:** We’ll see about that, Mr. Hawthorne. *Outside, the rain intensifies. Inside, time seems to slow. Jasper leafs through his book, sneaking glances at Gwen. She catches him once, and for a moment, neither looks away.* **JASPER:** (softly) It’s… nice in here. **GWEN:** It’s just a shop. **JASPER:** It’s more than that. *He says it like a promise. The bell above the door jangles again as a new customer enters, and the moment breaks. Gwen moves to greet them, but something lingers in the air between her and Jasper, as if the scene is not quite finished.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene is largely successful as a piece of charged romantic banter. Jasper's fragile ego is well drawn: his fishing for recognition ("You're not going to ask for a selfie?"), his visible flummoxing at Gwen's indifference, and the way her immunity paradoxically hooks him all track the brief faithfully. Gwen's deadpan wit ("I don't own a telly," the Bargain Hunt biscuits, custard cream autographs) is genuinely funny and characterful, and her reluctant selfie for her mum is a nice earned concession. The undercurrent of mutual attraction is present, mostly shown through beats and pauses rather than stated — though the narration occasionally tells ("Something unspoken passes between them," "despite herself, smiles"). Weaknesses: The prompt asked for prose "primarily in dialogue"; the model instead wrote a screenplay format, which is a deviation in form, though dialogue is indeed dominant. Cardiff is a city, not a small town, slightly undercutting the setting brief. Some elements are stock — the ginger cat, rain lashing windows, the smouldering actor, the "It's more than that" line — and the ending, with a new customer breaking the moment, is a familiar beat. Jasper's vulnerability ("Maybe forgetting's easier, sometimes") arrives quickly and feels a touch easy, though it's not wholly unearned. Gwen's Welshness is name-only; the Wales setting is thin beyond the name Gwenllian. Prose is clean and readable but not distinctive; within a screenplay format, prose quality is less testable. Length is slightly under 1000 words. Overall, a charming, competent, moderately clichéd scene with strong banter and a somewhat formulaic shape. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 68.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The underhold breathed with a cold, oily damp—the kind that clung to the inside of your lungs and left you tasting salt and rust. Aya’s boots echoed as she descended the spiral stairs, Katra’s hand firm on her shoulder, Simeon’s anxious breath loud behind. Gas lamps lined the stone corridor, their light trembling, painting monstrous silhouettes on the vaulted ceiling. The air stank of whale oil, iron, and old secrets. Aya’s palm itched with the urge to summon, to call forth something black and hungry from the immateria, but she forced her nerves into stillness. The corridor widened suddenly into a crypt-like chamber. Here, the walls were slabs of dark, weeping basalt, and the floor was slick with a sheen of spilled lamp oil. At the center: a dais, upon which rested the guild’s prize—a scythan relic, serpentine and cruel, its surface writhing with runes that seemed to crawl in the lamplight. But Aya’s eyes snapped to the far end of the room, where a familiar figure lounged on a throne of welded pipes and ribbed whale-bone. Mistress Marelle, the guild’s iron-fisted leader, alive and resplendent in a crimson frock-coat, her hands folded over a gleaming harpoon-cane. Two bodyguards flanked her, faces hidden by soot-black respirators, pistols glinting beneath their oilskin cloaks. Marelle’s voice cut through the hush like cold steel. “So. The rats descend to gnaw at the old cheese.” Her gaze flicked to Aya, then to Katra and Simeon. “You thought me caged, did you?” Aya felt Simeon stiffen at her side. Katra’s fingers tensed on her shoulder, but Aya stepped forward, mask firm on her face, voice low and calm. “We heard you’d been taken by the constables. Seems we were misinformed.” Marelle’s painted lips curled. “Oh, they *took* me, sweetling. But never believe a Morskan lock can hold a true daughter of the deep.” She snapped her fingers. The bodyguards advanced, pistols raised. Katra hissed, “Aya, we should—” But it was too late. From the shadows behind them, rough hands seized Simeon, wrenching his arms behind his back, and Katra found herself with a cold barrel pressed beneath her jaw. Aya, for her part, stood perfectly still, letting the guards strip the blade from her belt and wrench the mask from her face. The gaslight flickered over her features—aristocratic cheekbones, dark hair coiled with a single silver comb. Marelle’s eyes widened, the recognition cutting through all pretense. “Well, well. *Lady* Ayasha Varkova. The prodigal daughter come to slum it with the likes of us.” Marelle’s tone was silk stretched over steel. Aya’s heart hammered—her family’s name was poison here, a badge of privilege and betrayal. She straightened, refusing to give Marelle the satisfaction of seeing her squirm. Katra spat blood, glancing sidelong at Aya. “You know her?” Aya tried to keep her voice steady. “We’ve met. In other circumstances.” Marelle rose, cane tapping on the stone with a hollow ring. She circled Aya, eyes hungry. “You had us all fooled, didn’t you? Hiding behind that mask, playing at gutter games. But tell me, my little magicker: how much would your father pay to have you returned, heart beating and mind intact?” A tremor ran through Simeon. “Mistress, please—she’s worth more than—” “Silence!” Marelle’s voice cracked like a whip. The guards wrenched Simeon’s arms, and he fell to his knees. Aya fought to keep panic from her voice. “If you kill us, you’ll have nothing but trouble. The Varkovas have long memories. But if you let us walk, I can ensure you’re compensated—handsomely.” Marelle laughed, a low, wet sound. “Oh, sweetling, I don’t want your money. I want your *secrets*.” She leaned in, breath hot with gin and brine. “You’ve been dabbling, haven’t you? Immateria magick. The kind that gets girls hanged—like your mother.” Aya’s composure faltered at the mention of her mother—the image flashed, legs swinging, eyes wide and unseeing. She forced herself to meet Marelle’s gaze. “You know what I am. You also know what I can do. If you kill me, you’ll never learn how I called the shadows at the dock, never see the things I’ve bound in salt and blood. Keep me alive, and I’ll teach you.” Marelle considered this, head cocked. “And why would I trust a Varkova’s word?” Aya’s voice was soft, but it carried in the cold stone vault. “Because you want power, not vengeance. And power is what I can give.” A silence stretched, broken only by the hiss of the gas lamps and the distant groan of the city above, all gears and steam and the ceaseless roar of the whale-oil refineries. Aya felt the weight of her companions’ eyes—fear and accusation, hope and desperation. Katra spoke, voice raw. “Aya… what are you doing?” Aya didn’t answer. Her mind raced, sifting through half-remembered rituals, the taste of copper on her tongue, the old nursery rhymes her mother used to whisper in the dark. If she could buy them time—just a little—perhaps there was a way to turn this. Marelle straightened, cane tapping twice more. “Bind them. Take them below. And see to it our little magicker is kept somewhere… *special*.” She smiled, sharklike. “We have so much to discuss, Lady Varkova. So very much.” Rough hands seized Aya, twisting her arms behind her back. The flickering lamps cast their shadows long and monstrous as the trio were dragged deeper into the underhold. Aya’s mask lay discarded on the stone, its empty eyes staring up at the gaslight. She forced herself to remember the taste of salt and blood, the shape of her mother’s last spell, and hoped—prayed—that in the darkness below, she would find a way out. Marelle’s laughter followed them down the corridor, echoing off the basalt walls—a grim lullaby in the depths of the whale-lit city.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response fulfills the core brief competently: the trio enters the underhold, encounters the un-incarcerated guild leader (Mistress Marelle) with bodyguards, is captured without a fight scene, Aya is unmasked and revealed as aristocracy, and she negotiates on her value as a hostage/magicker while grappling internally with exposure. The whalepunk-Victorian texture is well established through whale oil, brass, gas lamps, respirators, and the "whale-lit city." Gothic horror elements are present but somewhat generic (weeping basalt, flickering lamps, monstrous shadows). Strengths: The scene structure is tight and purposeful; the pacing builds tension without meandering. Dialogue carries the confrontation well, and Marelle's voice—silky menace, theatrical cruelty—is the most distinct. Aya's internal monologue is integrated naturally, particularly the flash of her mother's hanging and the nursery-rhyme memories, which add emotional complexity. The negotiation is believable: Aya offers utility (secrets, magick instruction) rather than money, which fits her character and the world's fear of magicka. Weaknesses: The prose leans on stock phrases—"silk stretched over steel," "sharklike smile," "cracked like a whip," "cold steel"—which read as genre boilerplate. Katra and Simeon are thinly sketched; Simeon exists mainly to be silenced and kneed, Katra to ask questions. The unmasking moment, the story's emotional pivot, resolves too easily—Marelle's shock gives way to leverage almost instantly, deflating the stakes. The ending, with the trio dragged below and Marelle's laughter echoing, is atmospheric but conventional, and Aya's hope feels more authorial convenience than earned. Some telling creeps in ("Aya fought to keep panic from her voice," "her composure faltered"). The worldbuilding, while flavorful, doesn't surprise: the beats land exactly where a reader would predict. Overall: a solid, professional genre scene with good atmosphere and competent dialogue, but short of originality and emotional depth in its secondary characters and pivotal moments. Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Neon light leaks through grime-caked windows, painting Spike Spiegel’s face sickly green as he slouches at the counter, nursing his second glass of rotgut. He flicks his lighter, ignites a fresh cigarette, and exhales a cloud that blends into the haze already clinging to the ceiling. The bartender eyes him, but says nothing; the kind of trouble that follows men like Spike is best left undisturbed. The door creaks. Spike’s one good eye tracks the newcomer in the mirror behind the bar. She moves like she owns the place—boots heavy, hips swinging, a dragon tattoo glinting on her bare arm. Her cutoff shorts and crop top defy the city’s perpetual drizzle, and the twin pistols holstered at her hips draw more stares than her legs. She scans the room with a predator’s wariness, then drops onto the stool beside Spike. “Bar’s dead,” she grunts. “You scare off the locals, tall guy?” Spike smirks, lips barely twitching. “Guess they don’t like the smell of gun oil and cheap cologne.” Revy signals for a whiskey, downs it in one swallow. “You waiting for someone, or just hoping to drown in that glass?” He shrugs, rolling the cigarette between his lips. “Maybe both. Depends how the night goes.” His gaze lingers on the dragon winding around her arm. “Nice ink. Must hurt like hell.” “Pain’s just proof you’re alive.” She lights her own smoke, eyes narrowing. “So, you here for the same reason I am, or are you just another loser looking for a quick buck?” Spike’s laughter is low and lazy. “If you mean a bounty named Vasquez with a taste for explosives and bad poetry? Yeah. Though I’m starting to think competition’s going to make this less profitable.” She grins, all teeth and challenge. “I don’t split. You want him, you better be faster.” They size each other up—two wolves at the same kill. Under other circumstances, this could be a dance. As it is, it’s a standoff. The bartender coughs, sliding Revy another shot. She ignores him, leaning closer to Spike. Smoke curls between them. “You any good, or just another pretty face with a death wish?” Spike tips his glass to her. “A little of both. But I’m still breathing.” “Not for long if you cross me, cowboy.” He meets her glare, and for a moment, the air between them sizzles with something that isn’t quite hostility. “Whatever happens, happens,” he says. She snorts. “You sound like you already gave up.” “Just realistic.” Movement at the back—three thugs, Vasquez’s crew, by the looks of them. They recognize Spike and Revy at the same time, hands twitching toward their guns. Spike’s already moving, spinning off his stool, drawing his Jericho. Revy’s faster; both pistols clear leather, and she’s grinning as bullets fly. Glass shatters. The bartender dives for cover. Spike dives low, fires two rounds—one thug drops, clutching his leg. Revy dances sideways, firing from both hands, laughter bubbling up as she takes the second man in the shoulder. The third tries to run. Revy shoots the bottle from his hand, Spike kicks the door shut before he can escape. Silence falls, broken only by the ceiling fan’s lazy whir. Spike looks at her, breathless, smoke rising from his gun. “Not bad.” Revy holsters her pistols, grinning. “You’re slow, but you got style.” She steps over a groaning thug, snags a bottle off the bar, and gestures toward the alley. Spike follows, feeling the adrenaline in his veins like an old, familiar ache. # Rain drums on tin as they duck into a motel, the kind that rents by the hour and never asks questions. Revy slams the door behind them, drops the bottle on the nightstand. The room reeks of mildew and desperation. Spike lights another cigarette, tossing his coat over a chair. Revy paces, restless. “We could’ve taken Vasquez together. Instead, we’re playing chicken.” Spike stretches out on the bed, boots still on. “It’s not the job, it’s the company.” She glares. “Don’t get cute.” He grins, that lopsided, infuriating smile. “Can’t help myself.” Lightning flashes outside. Revy pours herself a drink, then another for Spike. She sits at the edge of the bed, close enough to smell the smoke on his skin. “You trust me?” she asks, voice low. Spike’s prosthetic eye glints. “Trust gets you killed.” He knocks back the shot. “But I don’t trust anyone, so you’re in good company.” She laughs, bitter. “Ain’t that the truth.” Tension coils in the silence—dangerous, electric. Her leg brushes his. He watches her, eyes heavy-lidded, lazy but alert. She’s beautiful and deadly, and he’s drawn to her recklessness like a moth to flame. She leans in, lips almost touching his. “You think you can take me?” His hand finds her wrist, slow and deliberate. “I could try. But you’d probably shoot me.” She grins, pressing the muzzle of her pistol against his ribs. “Only if you ask nice.” He laughs, low and genuine. “I like a woman who keeps me on my toes.” She cocks the hammer. His own gun is out, pressed to her thigh. For a moment, they are perfectly balanced—trustless, breathless, a hair’s breadth from violence or something else entirely. Outside, thunder shakes the windows. Inside, neither moves. Unresolved, the air between them is thick with the promise of gunfire or a kiss. Spike breaks the silence, voice soft. “I guess this means we’re partners.” She smirks, lowering her gun but not her guard. “Don’t get ahead of yourself, cowboy.” They sit in the half-light, guns low, hearts high, waiting to see which one blinks first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested scenario efficiently: seedy bar, mutual recognition, gunfight, motel standoff. Character voices are largely well-captured—Spike's fatalism and laziness, Revy's aggression and dark humor. The dialogue is snappy and mostly in character, though some lines lean on cliché ("pain's just proof you're alive," "moth to flame"). The gunfight is brisk and cinematic, and the final standoff achieves the requested tension, ending unresolved as specified. Weaknesses: the prose is competent but occasionally generic ("sizzles," "thick with promise"). The attraction is asserted more than developed—tension escalates quickly without much build. The thugs' arrival is a convenient plot device. Some imagery is stock noir without fresh detail. The ending is appropriately ambiguous, avoiding false positivity. No meandering; pacing is tight, though the ~1000-word target is roughly met.
