Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7999 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** Instances of SCP-7999-A (hereafter “SCP-7999 doors”) discovered globally are to be immediately secured and monitored by Foundation field teams. Civilian access is to be restricted under the cover story of hazardous material investigation. Mobile Task Force Epsilon-6 (“Village Idiots”) is tasked with investigating all newly reported SCP-7999-A manifestations and performing scheduled explorations of the SCP-7999-B archive. Personnel entering SCP-7999-B must undergo psychological evaluation pre- and post-entry. All documentation recovered within SCP-7999-B is to be cataloged and reviewed by RAISA (Records and Information Security Administration). Unauthorized access to SCP-7999-B, especially by Foundation personnel of Level 4 or higher, is to be reported directly to the O5 Council. **Description:** SCP-7999 refers to a phenomenon wherein identical, unmarked wooden doors (SCP-7999-A) appear in abandoned structures worldwide. All SCP-7999-A instances are physically identical, featuring no markings except for a pattern of deep scratches encircling the doorknob, consistent across all known examples. Opening an SCP-7999-A door leads to SCP-7999-B: a vast, architecturally anomalous archive, seemingly infinite in size and containing records, artifacts, and documentation not consistent with any known civilization. Recovered materials within SCP-7999-B reference a previous, global civilization (“The Former Custodians”), destroyed by an unspecified “containment failure.” Documents include references to a containment organization nearly identical to the modern SCP Foundation, though under alternate nomenclature (e.g., “The Custodial Collective”). Personnel files matching current Foundation staff, dated centuries prior, have been discovered. During exploration, Foundation teams have encountered humanoid entities (SCP-7999-C), uniformly garbed in yellow hazmat suits with no visible insignia. These entities are observed systematically removing sections of the archive. Attempts at communication result in rapid retreat; pursuit has been met with the entities’ disappearance into inaccessible sections. Security records indicate that several O5 Council members have accessed SCP-7999-B without proper authorization. Investigation is ongoing. --- **Addendum 7999-01: Exploration Logs** **Exploration Log 7999-B-04** *Team Lead: Dr. H. Navarro* *Team: MTF Epsilon-6* *Date: 2023-09-11* *Entry Point: SCP-7999-A instance, abandoned textile mill, Manchester, UK* **[BEGIN LOG]** **Navarro:** (Body cam flickers as the door opens) Confirming entry. Door opens into a corridor, wallpapered in green, stretching at least fifty meters, lined with filing cabinets. **Agent Kilpatrick:** Air's stale. No immediate threats. *(Team advances. The corridor widens into a massive rotunda. Ceiling height: 30 meters. Shelves spiral upward, filled with paper files, metallic cubes, and thick, leather-bound ledgers.)* **Navarro:** Team, prioritize documentation with legible language or recognizable symbols. *(Agent Kaur retrieves a folder marked “Custodial Collective: Personnel Records, 1746.”)* **Kaur:** Navarro, you need to see this. *(Camera focuses on a personnel file titled “Dr. Helena Navarro, Senior Archivist.” Attached is a photograph resembling the team lead, dated 1746.)* **Navarro:** (voice unsteady) This… can’t be possible. --- **Recovered Document Excerpt** *File: Custodial Collective Personnel Dossier* *Subject: Dr. Helena Navarro* *Date: 1746, Year of the Autumn Breach* > “Senior Archivist Navarro, assigned to Archive Delta, authorized for containment oversight of artifacts classified ‘Unthinkable.’ Clearance: O5-6. > Note: Subject recommended for memory reinforcement following the events of the Dawn Collapse.” --- **[LOG CONTINUED]** *(Team proceeds into a side chamber. Walls are lined with display cases containing artifacts: a melted clock, a glass sphere with shifting colors, and a rusted revolver labeled “Failure of Protocol 001.”)* **Kilpatrick:** Got movement. Two… no, three figures, northeast alcove. *(Entities in yellow hazmat suits are seen detaching a shelf labeled “Era of Survivors - Incident Reports.” They notice the team and immediately retreat, carrying documents into a darkened doorway that then vanishes.)* **Navarro:** Pursue! *(The team arrives at the vanished doorway; only a blank wall remains. No trace of the entities.)* **Kaur:** They’re systematically removing whole sections. Why? **Navarro:** Unknown. Take what we can and get out. --- **Addendum 7999-02: Recovered Documents** **Recovered Document Excerpt** *Title: “The Autumn Breach - Executive Summary”* *Source: Custodial Collective Archive* *Date: Redacted* > “The incident, now designated ‘Autumn Breach,’ resulted in the irreversible compromise of the global containment network. Civilizational collapse followed within 72 hours. Surviving Custodians initiated memory erasure and temporal displacement protocols. Reestablishment of containment organizations is imperative. > > Note: All records referencing the O5 Synod and their actions during the breach are to be sequestered in Archive Omega.” --- **Exploration Log 7999-B-08** *Team Lead: Dr. H. Navarro* *Team: MTF Epsilon-6* *Date: 2023-10-14* *Entry Point: SCP-7999-A, derelict hospital, Detroit, USA* **[BEGIN LOG]** *(Team enters a spiraling staircase. Descending, they pass murals depicting figures in containment uniforms facing monstrous silhouettes.)* **Kaur:** These look like… us. *(At sublevel 9, the team encounters a conference room. A long table is set with place cards labeled “O1” through “O13.” A recent-looking manila folder sits at “O5-2.”)* **Navarro:** That’s Foundation standard issue. *(Folder contains a sign-in sheet. Recent entries include “O5-2,” “O5-5,” and “O5-7.” Dates: three days prior.)* **Kilpatrick:** Council members have been coming here. Without authorization. *(Sudden motion detected. Two SCP-7999-C entities are seen carrying a large, locked box. One drops a slip of paper, which is retrieved by Agent Kaur.)* --- **Recovered Document Excerpt** *Handwritten Note:* > “They remember. We all do. The doors are thinning. The archive cannot remain. > > — O5-1” --- **[LOG CONTINUED]** **Navarro:** We’re leaving. Mark this location for additional surveillance. No further Council access without oversight. **[END LOG]** --- **Addendum 7999-03: Summary** Evidence strongly suggests that SCP-7999 is a remnant or echo of a prior anomalous containment structure, now collapsed. The persistence of personnel records referencing current Foundation staff in centuries-old documents implies possible identity recursion, memory alteration, or temporal displacement. The activities of SCP-7999-C entities indicate an ongoing effort to purge or salvage parts of the archive, perhaps to prevent further knowledge transfer, or as damage control. The unauthorized presence of O5 Council members within SCP-7999-B raises significant security concerns. Research is ongoing. All Foundation staff are advised: Should you encounter a door matching SCP-7999-A’s description—including deep scratches around the doorknob—do not attempt entry. Await MTF Epsilon-6. Further updates pending.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, well-structured SCP entry that hits every required beat: identical unmarked doors, the impossible archive, the destroyed prior civilization ("The Former Custodians"), the Foundation-under-another-name ("Custodial Collective"), personnel files of current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat entities removing sections and fleeing, and unauthorized O5 visits. The format is authentic — containment procedures, description, exploration logs, recovered document excerpts, addenda — and the third-person exploration-team perspective with document excerpts is executed as instructed. Length is roughly on target. Strengths: The worldbuilding details are effective and economical. "Year of the Autumn Breach," "Failure of Protocol 001" (a rusted revolver), the place cards "O1" through "O13," and the sign-in sheet dated three days prior are all strong, concrete artifacts that show rather than tell. The scratched doorknob motif is a nice unifying detail. The escalation across the two exploration logs is well-paced — from discovery of Navarro's own dossier to the conference room evidence of Council intrusion. The final handwritten note ("They remember. We all do.") lands as an effective, ominous closing beat. Weaknesses: The prose is functional but rarely elevated; descriptions are list-like ("a melted clock, a glass sphere with shifting colors, and a rusted revolver") rather than atmospheric. Dialogue is serviceable but flat — Kilpatrick and Kaur exist mostly to state observations ("They're systematically removing whole sections. Why?"). Navarro's reaction to her own 1746 dossier ("This… can't be possible") is the expected cliché and the moment is underexploited; a stronger piece would let that existential horror breathe or complicate it. The hazmat entities behave exactly as briefed with no texture beyond the prompt requirements. The "O5-1" note is a convenient, slightly contrived plot delivery. The summary addendum is somewhat redundant, restating what the logs already showed. There are no real surprises in structure — it follows the SCP template faithfully but predictably, and the deeper implications (identity recursion, memory erasure) are named rather than dramatized. Overall: a solid, professional genre piece with good artifact-level creativity, but limited atmosphere, flat characterization, and a tendency to summarize rather than inhabit its strangeness. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 54.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 5: The Glyph-Lit Streets of Selene’s Landing** It was the hour of second light, when the twin moons drew pale lines across the stone facades of Selene’s Landing. The young envoy, Maren Kestrel, slipped from the shadowed portico of the Guest House with only the faintest hesitation, boots echoing against the ancient stones. Official doctrine prescribed isolation: diplomats must not mingle, must not see, except through the arranged lenses of their hosts. Yet curiosity, like the slow patient water that carved the valleys of this world, was not so easily dammed. The city’s arteries ran with the low hum of commerce. Maren passed beneath arches carved with glyphs—spirals of sea and sky, figures with outstretched arms, faces that were neither quite human nor wholly other. Old Earth myths, the briefing had said, preserved in stone by hands that had never touched Earth. “They hold their heritage close,” the briefing had warned. “They are sensitive to implication.” Yet the markets did not feel sensitive, nor suspicious. Instead, they pressed in with scents of spiced root and smoke, and the polyphonic calls of vendors. Here, Maren saw the divergence not as dogma, but as fact: a woman with gilled neck and wide, limpid eyes sorted shellfruit with hands of impossible dexterity; a man, tall and sinewed, bore the high cheekbones and dense hair of the plateau lineages; a child, four-armed and laughing, darted between them, chased by a dog with a split tail. The envoy slowed, heart thudding. These were not the rigid castes the reports had described—“the aquatic, the highlanders, the adaptives”—but people, bartering over rootcakes, arguing over a torn piece of cloth, children making up rules to games. The city’s edges blurred the categories. From a high terrace, a group of elders watched the street. Their gaze followed Maren, appraising, but not hostile. The envoy offered a shallow nod, uncertain of the local customs. One elder, whose skin shimmered with a dusting of silver scales, returned the gesture with a slow, deliberate smile. Stone benches circled a fountain, itself carved with the myth of the First Ark: a vessel not of wood, but of bone and crystal, carrying humanity from the dying blue world to this one. The glyphs depicted the Ark’s crew—many-handed, many-eyed, diverse in form even then. Maren paused, tracing the lines with a gloved finger. The official briefings had not mentioned the Ark. A bell tolled, deep and resonant. The crowd shifted. Maren realized with a start how easily they could be lost here—how readily the city could fold them into its pattern, and how little the offworld protocols had prepared them for the living complexity of this place. ** * In the hush of their assigned quarters, Maren stood at the window, watching the city’s lights flicker. The commset chirped—a terse tone. Command. “You left the schedule,” the voice of Director Han was clipped, tired. “That’s not acceptable, Kestrel. We have protocols for a reason.” Maren tried to explain—the glyphs, the living market, the sense that something in the briefings was incomplete—but was cut off. “Your task is to meet with Minister Ral. The Science Ministry holds the data we need. Do not deviate again. Understood?” “Yes, Director.” The line went dead. ** * Minister Ral’s office occupied the uppermost chamber of the Observatory, a dome of polished stone etched with constellations. The Minister was waiting, a tall figure robed in indigo, skin marked with patterns that shifted as they moved—an artifact, perhaps, of the planetary adaptation. Ral’s eyes—silver, unblinking—regarded Maren with the patience of a scientist, the cunning of a politician. “You are younger than I expected,” Ral said, voice low and rough-edged. Maren inclined their head. “Younger than most diplomats, perhaps. But I am here to listen, and to learn.” “A rare virtue, in your kind.” Ral gestured to a pair of stone seats. “Please. Let us begin.” The chamber was cool. The only sound was the soft whir of ventilation, and the distant clangor of bells from the city below. “I have read your briefings,” Ral began. “You are here to ‘address tensions.’ To ‘facilitate dialogue.’ You wish to understand why the colony resists reintegration. You want to know why we refuse homogenization—why we do not wish to be made one species again.” Maren hesitated. “I’m here to understand your position, Minister. Not to force it.” Ral’s lips curled. “You walked our streets today. Against your Command’s wishes.” It was not a question. Maren said nothing. “Tell me what you saw.” Maren gathered their thoughts. “I saw a city that is not divided as we were told. The lineages are interwoven. The glyphs on your arches—they show the Ark as a vessel for all, not just one kind.” Ral’s gaze sharpened. “You notice glyphs? Most offworlders see only the differences.” “I noticed the differences, too. But I also saw a child with four arms and a man with gills buying the same rootcakes.” Ral tipped their head. “Good. Then let us speak plainly. Your Command fears what we have become. They wish to erase our differences, to make us—what? Homo sapiens, mark two? They do not see that divergence is our strength.” Maren nodded. “But the briefings say there are tensions. That the lineages compete for resources, that integration is breaking down.” Ral’s eyes flashed. “There are always tensions, envoy. What society has none? But we manage them. The troubles come not from within, but from without—when offworlders insist we conform, when they try to dictate what it means to be human.” Maren leaned forward. “The glyphs—why do you preserve the old myths?” Ral’s smile was slow. “Because memory is a kind of future. The Ark was not a ship, but a promise: that humanity could become many things. We carve the glyphs to remind ourselves that we are still on that voyage.” Silence stretched between them. Maren felt the weight of the city pressing in—the living complexity of the markets, the silent judgement of the elders, the echo of Command’s demands. “Will you report what you saw?” Ral asked, softly. Maren met the Minister’s gaze. “I will report the truth.” Ral studied them for a long moment. “Perhaps you are not like the others. Perhaps.” Outside, the bells of Selene’s Landing tolled again, and the glyph-lit walls seemed to shimmer with the promise of stories yet untold.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece follows the prompt's structure faithfully: the unauthorized street walk, the market encounters revealing divergence, the reprimand from Command, and the testing conversation with Minister Ral. The Le Guin influence shows in the anthropological bent—the glyphs, the First Ark myth, the emphasis on culture over action—and in the theme of divergence-as-strength, which echoes The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed. Strengths: The prose is generally clean and controlled, with some genuinely nice images (the twin moons, the fountain carving of the Ark, "memory is a kind of future"). The market scene does effective work showing rather than telling the divergence, and the child with four arms buying rootcakes beside a gilled woman is a good Le Guin-esque detail of ordinariness amid strangeness. The dialogue with Ral has moments of genuine political texture—Ral's pivot from testing to cautious respect is well-handled. Weaknesses: The piece is competent but somewhat safe and schematic. The plot beats arrive exactly as expected: the envoy sees truth, is reprimanded, passes the test, earns provisional respect. Ral's "test" lacks real teeth—there's no moment where Maren genuinely falters or is cornered; the "wits and will tested" requirement is satisfied more by assertion than by dramatic pressure. The reprimand scene is thin and perfunctory. The ending ("stories yet untold") is a soft, unearned poetic flourish that gestures at depth without delivering it. Some phrasing is stock ("heart thudding," "eyes flashed," "lips curled"), and the worldbuilding, while pleasant, stays at the level of decorative detail—the subspecies are rendered as exotic traits rather than as social structures with real consequences. The "tensions" the envoy was sent to address remain abstract throughout, so the stakes never sharpen. The Le Guin voice is imitated in mannerism more than in rigor. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 64.1
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter 7: Polymerase Chain Reaction A ruddy dawn bled through the ragged slats of the settlement’s greenhouse, painting the makeshift laboratory in streaks of copper and pale gold. The solar rig on the roof, patched together from cracked panels and wire scavenged from the bones of abandoned electric cars, spat erratically into the charge controller. Every few minutes, the lights would flicker; every hour, the PCR thermocycler would complain with a shrill, dying beep, like a canary in a mine choking on its last breath. Mara hunched over the battered workbench, eyes gritty from a sleepless night. Her hands, callused and stained with iodine, moved with the practiced caution of someone who had watched too many friends wither from a single slip of the pipette. She coaxed a droplet of precious, viscous polymerase into a PCR tube—one of the last few she had, scavenged from the ruins of an old university, the labels long since worn away. The DNA sample she was working with glimmered faintly in the tube’s blue glow. It was ancient, by corporate standards—six months old, pulled from the core of a genetically engineered maize seed. The corporations had ensured that their patented DNA would last only a single generation, burning out like the fuse on a firecracker. It was their profit model: built-in obsolescence, even for life itself. The seeds you bought from them grew, but their offspring were sterile or simply failed to thrive, their gene-edited code unraveling into useless junk. Mara’s people had been living on dwindling stores, their diets a patchwork of old-world grains, foraged roots, and the occasional black-market miracle. She checked the thermocycler—an ancient, boxy thing, its casing cannibalized from a microwave oven, its heating element controlled by a Raspberry Pi spitting code that sometimes froze mid-cycle. The display flickered. She tapped the side, swore softly, and watched the temperature tick upward, praying the power would hold. A shadow fell across the polycarbonate door. Mara tensed. The settlement was small, and most people respected the sanctity of her lab; but black market contracts were a different matter. She reached for the scalpel under her bench—a reflex, nothing more. The door creaked open, letting in a breath of mold and charcoal smoke. A man stepped inside, his face half-hidden by a ragged scarf. He moved like someone who was used to being watched, shoulders hunched, gaze darting. He set a battered cooler on the bench with a thunk. “You Mara?” he asked. She nodded, not bothering with small talk. Two weeks ago, she’d received a message on the old meshnet—a contract for food crop edits, time-sensitive, high-risk. Payment in lithium batteries and a vial of antibiotics, both worth more than gold. The settlement needed the batteries; Mara needed the medicine. He unlatched the cooler. Inside were a handful of shriveled tomatoes, their skins patched with bruises and mold. But inside, if she was lucky, was the last faint echo of the engineered gene—the one for blight resistance, designed to die with the first harvest. If she could fish it out, PCR it up, splice it into local rootstock—they’d eat for another season. “Payment first,” she said, voice flat. He slid a wrapped bundle across the bench. The batteries clinked reassuringly; the antibiotic vial, sealed and clear, was a promise against infection. Mara pocketed them both without ceremony. “I’ll need six hours,” she said. “Power’s iffy.” He nodded, eyes flickering to the solar rig’s charge display—already dipping into the red. When he left, Mara set to work. She cracked open the tomatoes, scraping the pulp into a centrifuge cobbled from a bicycle wheel and scavenged bearings. The rhythm of the crank steadied her nerves. She poured off the liquid, pipetted a thread of DNA into the PCR tubes, and set the thermocycler for a desperate thirty cycles. She’d spliced in a viral promoter—untested, unstable, but maybe enough to make the gene stick in the next host. As the machine whined and clicked, Mara checked her own arm. The skin there was puckered and pink, a legacy of last month’s experiment—a homemade CRISPR patch meant to boost her immune system after a brush with septic water. It had worked, more or less; the fever had broken, but her muscles still twitched at odd hours, and she’d developed a taste for bitter greens she’d never liked before. Some of the others who’d tried her mods had fared worse: hair falling out in clumps, odd rashes, a sudden allergy to sunlight. The price of biohacking with half-melted reagents and expiry-dated enzymes. Yet there were upsides. The new recruits, fresh from the city’s collapse, marveled at how Mara’s cohort could digest almost anything—acorn flour, pine bark, even the tough, stringy weeds that choked the settlement’s fields. A side effect, perhaps, of generations of black market mods and scavenged corporate DNA. They were becoming something new, shaped by desperation and ingenuity. The thermocycler beeped. Mara pried open the lid, sweat prickling her brow as she checked the gel—another jury-rigged relic, powered by a car battery and cooled with melted snow. The bands were faint, but they were there: fragments of the blight-resistance gene, just enough to work with. She prepped the ligation mix, hands trembling with fatigue and hope. A drop of the viral vector, a sliver of salvaged maize DNA, a whisper of prayer to whatever gods still listened. She injected the mix into a batch of seedling rootstock, their green shoots trembling in the half-light. Outside, the sky brightened; the solar rig buzzed with new energy. In a few weeks, if the edit held, there would be tomatoes again—blight-resistant, patched together from the ruins of a broken world. Mara slumped onto her stool, exhaustion washing over her. Her muscles ached—the legacy of another genetic tweak gone sideways. But she was alive, and her people would eat. When the client returned, Mara handed over a tray of edited seedlings. “They should hold for a generation,” she said, voice hoarse. “After that—who knows?” The man’s eyes softened. “One generation’s enough, these days.” In the flickering light of the jury-rigged lab, surrounded by the ghosts of old machines and the promise of new life, Mara allowed herself a rare smile. In a world built on obsolescence, survival was the ultimate act of rebellion.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter fulfills the brief efficiently: post-apocalyptic biopunk setting, engineered obsolescence as corporate profit model, jury-rigged lab equipment (microwave-cased thermocycler, bicycle-wheel centrifuge, Raspberry Pi controller), physical tolls and unexpected upsides of self-administered gene mods, and a black market contract driving the plot. World-building details are the strongest element—concrete, tactile, and plausible without drowning the reader in jargon. Weaknesses: the prose leans on stock post-apocalyptic furniture (ragged scarf, "whatever gods still listened," "survival was the ultimate act of rebellion") and the closing line is a familiar aphorism that flattens an otherwise grounded ending. The client is a cipher; his "eyes softened" moment is unearned sentimentality. Dialogue is serviceable but flat—functional exchanges without distinct voice. Mara is competent and sympathetic but not deeply layered; her fatigue and fear are stated more than dramatized. The plot resolves without friction—the PCR works, the splice works, the client returns amiably—so tension evaporates rather than builds. Some telling ("The rhythm of the crank steadied her nerves") and a few clichés ("like a canary in a mine choking on its last breath") push toward overwrought without tipping fully into purple. The "taste for bitter greens" and digestive upsides are nice specific touches that earn the prompt's "unexpected upsides." Overall: solid, professional genre writing with good world-building, held back by predictable beats, thin characterization, and an ending that gestures at uplift it hasn't quite earned.
